\chapter{Five More Things You Ask For --- Knife, Cup, Pot, Blanket, Broom}
\label{ch:cinco-cosas-mas}
\hlchaptermodality{294}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for a knife, a cup, a pot, a blanket and a broom in Spanish, politely.}

Complete ES-C294-escoba: ask for all five in turn, with por favor on the end of each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el cuchillo]{el cuchillo — the little blade behind cutlery}

\label{lesson:ES-C294-cuchillo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what was \emph{tuber}? (A swelling.) And what was \emph{rota}? (A wheel.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cuchara — the one that does not cut.
  \item por favor — what you put on the end when you ask.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cu-CHI-llo}, stress in the middle. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in English \emph{church}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cuchillo} — \textquotedblleft{}the knife.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{culter} was a blade; \textbf{cultellus} was a small one. Spanish took the small one and forgot the big one, exactly as it did with the onion.

English took \emph{culter} by several roads at once. \textbf{Cutlery} came through French \emph{coutel}. A \textbf{cutlass} is \emph{coutelas}, an oversized one. And the \textbf{coulter} on a plough — the blade that cuts the soil ahead of the share — is the bare Latin word, still doing farm work.

You already have \emph{la cuchara}. It looks like a relative of \emph{cuchillo} and is not one: \emph{cuchara} is from \textbf{cochlearium}, a snail-shell spoon. Two kitchen words that begin with the same three letters and come from opposite places, which is a useful reminder that resemblance is not evidence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more thing you can ask for at a meal.

You had \emph{la cuchara} and \emph{el plato} already. Adding \emph{el cuchillo} means you can now ask for the two halves of the job — the thing that cuts and the thing that lifts — with nothing but \emph{por favor} on the end.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cuchillo}
  \item \emph{un cuchillo, por favor}
  \item \emph{la cuchara} and \emph{el cuchillo} — near neighbours, unrelated
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{culter}? (A blade.) What did \emph{cultellus} add? (Smallness.) And is \emph{cuchara} from the same word? (No — it is a snail shell.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la taza]{la taza — a cup that came a very long way}

\label{lesson:ES-C294-taza}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what was \emph{tuber}? (A swelling.) And what was \emph{cultellus}? (A little blade.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el vaso — the one you drink cold things from.
  \item el agua — what goes in either.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TA-za}, stress on the first part. The \emph{z} is the \emph{s} sound across most of the Spanish-speaking world. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la taza} — \textquotedblleft{}the cup.\textquotedblright{}

Another one with no Latin behind it. Arabic \textbf{tassa} brought it into Spain, and Arabic had it from Persian \textbf{tašt}, a bowl or a basin. So the word crossed two languages and most of a continent before it reached a Spanish kitchen.

French took the same Arabic word and made \textbf{tasse}, which is why a small strong coffee is served in a \textbf{demitasse} — a half-cup — in English restaurants that would not otherwise admit to speaking Persian.

Set this beside \emph{el vaso}, which you already have. \emph{Vaso} is Latin \textbf{vas}, a vessel, and gives English \textbf{vase} and \textbf{vascular}. Two drinking containers, sitting side by side in the same cupboard, from two completely different worlds.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the five, and both of them ask well.

\emph{Un cuchillo, por favor.} \emph{Una taza, por favor.} The polite frame has not changed since you first learned it — you are simply dropping new words into a shape you already trust, which is the cheapest kind of progress there is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la taza}
  \item \emph{una taza, por favor}
  \item \emph{el vaso} and \emph{la taza} — Rome and Persia in one cupboard
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language handed \emph{taza} to Spanish? (Arabic.) And before that? (Persian.) What is a \emph{demitasse}? (A half-cup.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la olla]{la olla — the word that never changed}

\label{lesson:ES-C294-olla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which language handed \emph{taza} to Spanish? (Arabic.) And what was \emph{culter}? (A blade.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el arroz — what goes in it.
  \item la cebolla — and what goes in with it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{O-lla}, two beats, stress on the first. The \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} sound; do not let the English \emph{l} creep in. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la olla} — \textquotedblleft{}the pot.\textquotedblright{}

There is nothing to take apart. Latin \textbf{olla} meant a cooking pot, and two thousand years later Spanish says \emph{olla} and means a cooking pot. Every letter is where the Romans left it.

That is rarer than it sounds, and it tends to happen to the humblest words. Grand Latin words get replaced, borrowed over, or refined into something abstract. A pot stays a pot because people keep needing one.

English does have it, at one remove. The Spanish dish \textbf{olla podrida} — literally a rotted pot, meaning a stew of everything — was borrowed into English as \textbf{olio}, a mixture. The French translated the name rather than borrowing it, and got \textbf{pot pourri}, which is the same two words again and now means a bowl of dried petals.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and a small point about how languages age.

\emph{El cuchillo} shrank, \emph{la taza} travelled, \emph{la olla} sat still. Three words from one kitchen, and three completely different fates — which is most of what etymology has to teach, in one cupboard.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la olla}
  \item \emph{el arroz en la olla}
  \item \emph{el cuchillo}, \emph{la taza}, \emph{la olla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How much has \emph{olla} changed since Latin? (Nothing at all.) What does \emph{olla podrida} mean literally? (A rotted pot.) And what did French make of it? (\emph{Pot pourri}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la manta]{la manta — a cloak that lay down}

\label{lesson:ES-C294-manta}



\begin{quote}
Quick pass: how much has \emph{olla} changed? (Nothing.) Which language gave \emph{taza}? (Arabic.) And what was \emph{cultellus}? (A little blade.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cama — where one lives.
  \item la toalla — the other useful cloth.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MAN-ta}, stress on the first part. Two clean beats, and the \emph{n} closes the first. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la manta} — \textquotedblleft{}the blanket.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mantum} was a cloak — something you wore. Spanish kept the cloth and dropped the wearing, so a \emph{manta} is now what goes over a bed rather than over your shoulders.

The cloak is still visible in English. A \textbf{mantle} is a cloak, literal or inherited: a bishop's, or a champion's. A \textbf{mantelpiece} is the shelf over a fire, named because the hood above the hearth was thought of as its cloak. A \textbf{mantilla} is a Spanish lace veil, and there is the small ending again. And a \textbf{manta ray} is named for its shape — a swimming cloak, which is the best description of one anybody has managed.

Spanish also has \emph{manto} for the cloak proper. So the language kept both: the masculine one stayed a garment, the feminine one lay down on a bed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four things to ask for, and a whole room implied by them.

\emph{El cuchillo}, \emph{la taza}, \emph{la olla}, \emph{la manta}. A kitchen and a bed between them. These are the words you actually need when you are a guest in somebody's house and do not want to rummage.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la manta}
  \item \emph{una manta, por favor}
  \item \emph{el cuchillo}, \emph{la taza}, \emph{la olla}, \emph{la manta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{mantum}? (A cloak.) Why is a mantelpiece called that? (The hood over the fire was its cloak.) And why is the manta ray called one? (It is shaped like a swimming cloak.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la escoba]{la escoba — the one with no English cousin}

\label{lesson:ES-C294-escoba}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{mantum}? (A cloak.) How much has \emph{olla} changed? (Nothing.) And what was \emph{culter}? (A blade.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item limpio — what this makes a room.
  \item sucio — what a room is before you use it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-CO-ba}, stress in the middle. The \emph{e-} step in front of \emph{sc}, and the \emph{b} between vowels is soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la escoba} — \textquotedblleft{}the broom.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{scopa} was a twig, and \textbf{scopae} in the plural was a bundle of them tied to a stick. That is what a broom was, and in much of the world still is.

Take the \emph{e-} off and \emph{scopa} is showing. That is the third time the step has earned its keep in this stretch — a star, a back, and now a broom.

Here is the honest part: this one has no everyday English relative. \emph{Scopa} stayed in Latin and in botany, and English built its own word from the broom plant instead. Most of the words in this book have arrived with a cousin attached, and it is worth meeting one that has not, so that the method does not start to look like magic. Sometimes a word is simply a word, and you learn it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el cuchillo}, \emph{la taza}, \emph{la olla}, \emph{la manta}, \emph{la escoba}.

Every one of them fits the asking-frame you already had, so the five cost you no grammar whatever. Four came with an English relative and the fifth came without one, which is a fair sample of how the vocabulary of a language is actually distributed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la escoba}
  \item \emph{una escoba, por favor}
  \item all five — \emph{el cuchillo}, \emph{la taza}, \emph{la olla}, \emph{la manta}, \emph{la escoba}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{scopa}? (A twig, and a bundle of them.) What is the \emph{e-} doing on the front? (Giving the tongue a start before \emph{sc}.) And does this one have an English cousin? (No — and that is worth knowing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
